text: Hello everyone, and welcome.

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Before we dive into the deep technical details of our AI platform, let us give you some essential context about Flywire.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Flywire is built to process the world's most complex payments across global industries like education, healthcare, travel, and business services.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Today, we serve over 5,000 clients across more than 240 countries around the world.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: They are core requirements of our business.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We operate under strict compliance frameworks like PCI, DSS, and SOC2.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This means that customer data, personal identification, and payment details must remain completely safe.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We cannot simply take sensitive context and pass it to third-party services without strict governance and architectural boundaries.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: To give you an idea of our engineering organization, we have around 400 software engineers distributed globally.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Across our teams, we maintain diverse technology stacks, including Java, Ruby, Go, Python, .NET, and PHP.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Almost everything we build and run is deployed on Victoria, our internal platform as a service that operates on top of GitLab and AWS infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Victoria provides standardized build pipelines and consistent deployment practices.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So, how did our AI journey begin?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: About six months ago, back in April, we formally established the dedicated AI platform experience team.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Even before that, passionate engineers across Flywire were already experimenting with AI tools, creating skills, building MCP servers, and assembling an early code review bot.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That organic activity proved that our engineers wanted AI automation.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It also showed that we needed a dedicated team to provide infrastructure for safe and reliable agendic solutions.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Since then, we have moved fast with close to a thousand commits to our internal tool.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But the industry does not stop.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In the same six months, Claude Code alone published more than 160 releases, almost one per day.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And the major AI labs released more than 20 new models.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Every week brings a new model and a new tool or a new way of working.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Our challenge is not only to build fast, but to keep up.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This brings us to Orbit, our own toy killer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Orbit is an internal platform that eliminates daily engineering repetitive tasks by including LLMs directly into structured workflows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Instead of letting AI agents run freely in open-ended loops, Orbit pairs deterministic code with small LLM steps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We crystallize repetitive procedural logic into code, and we call a model only where reasoning is actually needed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we evaluated whether to build or buy, building in-house made complete sense for our environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Frontier models made feature development really fast, which drastically lowers the cost of a custom platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: More importantly, as a financial enterprise handling PCI, PAI, and PHI data, keeping execution inside our existing Victoria infrastructure ensures that sensitive data never leaves our control environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also skip long vendor security reviews and extra compliance work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what does a workflow actually look like?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every agent in orbit is defined in a single JML file that lives in our repository and goes through the same merge request review as any other code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Take our code review agent as an example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It starts with a trigger,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A Gilda webhook that fires when an engineer mentions the review bot on a merge request.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: From there, a sequence of deterministic activities fetches the merge request metadata, classifies its risk tier, loads prior findings, and clones the repository.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Only then, we call the model, in an LLM step that can read the code but has no permission to modify it, and that must answer in a strict output schema.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Finally, another deterministic step, pose the findings back to the met request.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is what we mean by workflows, not autopilot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Code handles the predictable parts, and the model is called only where reasoning is actually needed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We choose to start with YAML files and a met request review process on purpose.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: YAML is a format our engineers already know, and the review works the way they already work every day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It also keeps the codebase AI friendly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Coding agents can read, write, and review workflow definitions as easily as people can.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: However, not every use case comes from an engineering team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For corporate use cases, we are considering an authoring tool in the Orbit UI, where people can build a workflow by dragging and dropping from a set of predefined activities, without writing in a YAML.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A workflow can start in three ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Engineers and other systems can call Orbit's internal API directly or using our internal CLI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Webhooks from GitLab, Jira, Sentry, and AWS start a workflow from the moment something happens, such as a new merge request or a new production error.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Scheduled jobs run workflows on a fixed cadence, like our daily translation syncs, feature flag cleanups, and knowledge-based refreshes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Beyond these entry points, we are currently building an MCP server for Orbit so that the other AI services and tools we use across Flywire can start workflows directly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, an engineer will be able to ask Claude in Slack through Claude Tag to run an Orbit workflow without ever leaving the conversation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We started small, with clear high-impact use cases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, the daily engineering work, automated code reviews on merge requests, and our Victoria upgrades agent, which fixes Victoria linter findings automatically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, translations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One workflow now handles the full cycle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It fetches the new strings, translates them, updates the files, and notifies the teams with the updated docs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, production errors.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A Sentry webhook starts the Sentry investigator.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It assesses the issue, posts the assessment in Slack, and shares the mail request with the fix in the same place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: On the support side, TicketTriage classifies new tickets and routes them to the right engineering area.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: AI Readiness Scorecards measures how ready a repository is for AI-assisted development, and a fixer acts on the findings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Finally, the Jira implementer takes a ticket and turns it into a merge request.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It works like a small software factory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the biggest benefits that we found is that we can make changes in bulk across many repositories.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That lets us do software engineering at scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It is very convenient for migrations, library updates, and deprecations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we also use it to run Claude Doctor and to launch
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Our own AI Readiness Scorecard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even with all this automation, the merge request is still our unit of work, and it is where a human stays in the loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We operate in a regulated environment, so people still review and approve those merge requests.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's take a deeper look at the technical architecture of Orbit.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Originally, we began with a simple container setup on AWS ECS Fargate, where the orchestration layer harness and the runtime environment lived inside the same container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: As our needs grew, we evolved towards separating the orchestration layer, the agent runtime environment, and the session state into distinct components.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This improves isolation, maintainability, and resource allocation.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It also makes the system more resilient, because an error in the effort does not kill the sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it lets us scale each piece independently and adapt to changing requirements.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Fargate lets us scale tasks elastically so we can run a very large number of agents in parallel.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It was also really easy to deploy Arbit, because we already had Victoria, our path that scales applications without any effort.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But that scale needs guardrails, so the platform is not misused.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: First, timeouts.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Every agent stops after a configurable amount of time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Second, rate limits, which are aggressive by default.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A broken API integration could start spawning thousands of agents and make our build much bigger.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The limits keep that under control.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Third, concurrency control.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Our control plane uses logs to prevent duplicate executions of the same task.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: For example, if a code review is already running, we drop the duplicated request.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Running agents inside Victoria comes with container limits.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Victoria uses standard Fargate task definitions, so the containers are lightweight and tightly restricted.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Our baseline agent container includes the common language runtimes, but it intentionally leaves out package managers like Bundler, Maven, and Composer.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So heavy agents, like our Jira implementer, cannot easily run native builds or unit tests inside the container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When we started Orbit in April, AWS Lambda micro VMs did not exist yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: AWS released them in June, so our first version ran only on Fargate.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: These are managed micro VMs that work like Lambda functions, reasonable processes, so they can pause and continue where they stop.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That fits the nature of agent execution really well, so we now use them with a runtime chosen by project type.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Each tech stack gets its own tool chain quickly in an isolated environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This is not full sandboxing yet, and we are actively moving there.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The goal is to support setups like Docker in Docker or multiple micro VMs so agents can run tests or more complex verifications on any repository.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Inside each LLM step, we did not build our own harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Instead, we reused the Claude Agents SDK, the same harness that powers Claude Code.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This gives us a mature, well-tested harness with tool usage, sub-agents, and skills out of the box, so we can focus on the workflow rather than on the plumbing.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: What we add on top is control.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We restrict four different things for every step.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The network the agent can reach, the tools it can call, the skills it can load, and the MCP servers it can use, down to the specific tools allowed from each server.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: All of this is declared in the YAML file itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A code review step, for example, can read and search the code but cannot edit files or push changes.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And our central investigator can query traces through our MCP server, but only with a short list of read-only tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In practice, each of them step runs with only the access it needs and the access is visible and reviewable like any other code.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Skills themselves come from a single place.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: At Flywire, we maintain a central repository of skills that is published internally as a Claude Code Plugin Marketplace, and Orbit connects to that marketplace at build time.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This means the same skills works in two places.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: An engineer can run it in Claude Code on their laptop, and Orbit can run it inside an automated workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That shared foundation also shapes our recommendation to teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Start with the skill.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Skill is cheap to write, easy to iterate on, and useful from day one.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Once a team is sure that a task is worth automating, we move it into Orbit and turn it into workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The predictable parts become deterministic code.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The model is called only where it adds value, and each run becomes more reliable and less expensive than an open-ended session.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Workflows also run in the background, so engineers do not have to sit with an open session and guided step-by-step.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That means less context switching and more time for the work that needs them.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Beyond runtime isolation, we also rely heavily on structure output to guarantee systemic reliability.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Every LLM step in an orbit workflow enforces strict JSON schemas for model responses.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: By constraining output formats, we ensure that subsequent execution branches, error handling, and state transitions are driven by deterministic control flow rather than unpredictable string parsing.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: If an LLM response fails validation against the expected JSON schema, ORBIT automatically triggers a targeted retry or fallback pass before proceeding.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Another crucial pattern we rely on is isolated component evaluation.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Evaluating complex, end-to-end agentic workflows in synthetic benchmark environments is often noisy, expensive, and difficult to reproduce consistently.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Instead of trying to evaluate entire workflows from start to finish, our evaluation harness isolates individual LLM steps.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: By injecting exact historical state and context directly into specific workflow nodes, we can evaluate model output quality, measure PROM adjustments, and catch performance regressions quickly and cost effectively.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So how do we know that an agent is good enough?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Today, a new agent usually reaches production after a vibe check.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The team tries it on a few real cases and confirms that it behaves as expected.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Once it runs in production, we trace every execution end-to-end with OpenTelemetry, including each activity, model call, and tool call.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We then extract traces from real executions and add them to a golden dataset.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: For now, each golden dataset is versioned in the repository next to the code, and we run it on demand.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Based on those results, we improve the prompt or change the model, and we run the dataset again to compare.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We do not have online evaluations yet, but we are working on them internally.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Our goal is to run the whole evaluation loop inside Orbit from the UI or through the MCP server.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: First, you deploy your agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Then, you monitor and evaluate its execution in production.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Finally, you improve the agent based on those evaluations without the need to deploy it again.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That is our roadmap for evaluations.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: One place to ship, measure, and improve every workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The operational impact of this approach has been significant across our engineering organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In the past 30 days alone, our automated code review agent completed over 9,700 runs, averaging under three minutes per merge request.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Beyond CodeReview, our AuditFixer opened 159 merge requests to fix vulnerable dependencies and the AI ReadinessFixer improved around 80 repositories.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The VictoriaLinterFixer fixed 413 projects and the MergeConflictResolver ran 921 times.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Across these workflows, we ran over 11,000 executions with a 99% success rate.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Reflecting on our journey, adopting a self-service model was one of the best decisions we've made.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Standardized guardrails allow engineers across SRE, security, IT, and support to build custom workflow steps easily and safely.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also learned that cost control starts with model selection.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not every step needs the most capable model, so each LLM step in a workflow declares its own model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, a planning step and an implementation step can use different models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Matching the model to the task keeps cost under control, and it is why a cost-aware model router is in our roadmap.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: On the other hand, managing data separation remains an ongoing responsibility.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We maintain a strict isolation between engineering SDLC data, corporate operational data, and sensitive payment production data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Additionally, because demand for automation is high, maintaining focus and prioritizing high-impact work is essential.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Looking ahead, our roadmap focuses on expanding our platform features and increasing overall architecture flexibility.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are actively moving towards a complete sandboxing so agents can handle complex builds, local environments, and test suite seamlessly across all project types.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Moving forward, we are also introducing resumable sessions to handle complex multi-step tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are also building more evaluation tools directly into orbit so teams can measure the quality of their workflows on the platform itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In parallel, we are refactoring our orchestration layer to be model agnostic, enabling flexible routing across different model vendors, including an automated model router that selects the most cost-effective model for each task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That will help us control cost as we keep scaling the platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also want to make the platform harness agnostic so that we are not tied to a single harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To wrap up, here are three things we learn.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, start small.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pick a repetitive, well-defined task and prove it works before you scale it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, use the model only where it adds value.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everything predictable stays as code, and that is what keeps the workflows reliable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And third, keep guardrails and humans in the loop, owners' limits and met request reviews.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That is how we move from AI experiments to workflows our engineers use every day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you all so much for your time and attention today.
